Coach Bubista is lifted into the air after Cabo Verde secured its unlikely place in the World Cup knockouts. (Getty Images: Rico Brouwer/Soccrates)

Cabo Verde secured second spot in its World Cup group with three draws, finishing ahead of Uruguay and Saudi Arabia.

It is the first time the small island nation off the western coast of Africa has played at the World Cup.

Cabo Verde next faces reigning World Cup champions Argentina on July 3.

Cabo Verde completed an improbable run through the group stage with a third straight World Cup draw to become the smallest country to earn a spot in the knockout round after a 0-0 draw against Saudi Arabia.

The small island nation off the western coast of Africa, which is making its debut on football's grandest stage, had already held 2010 champion Spain to a 0-0 draw and then came from behind to get a 2-2 result against Uruguay.

Cabo Verde's three points put the team in second place behind Spain, which beat Uruguay and won the group.

Cabo Verde will play reigning World Cup champion Argentina in Miami on July 3.

Cabo Verde players celebrate after learning that Uruguay had lost to Spain. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

Drawing all three group matches does not guarantee advancement at major football tournaments. But several teams have done it in the past, including Wales in 1958, Ireland and the Netherlands in 1990, and Chile in 1998.

New Zealand, however, also got three draws at the 2010 World Cup and was eliminated.

On the eve of the match, Cabo Verde coach Bubista mused, "Everyone is entitled to dream and nothing is impossible."

The Blue Sharks proved him right, overcoming seemingly insurmountable odds as the country of just more than 500,000 reached the round of 32.

A woman, her face painted with a flag of the archipelago, held a sign that read: "Small Islands, Big Dreams."

A fan holds a "small island, big dreams" sign in the crowd. (Getty Images)

It is a dream that the underdogs have made reality as they continue their charmed run on the world stage.

They did it with another strong game from Vozinha, the 40-year-old goalkeeper whose tournament success has helped him amass more than 16 million Instagram followers.

He had a save in first-half stoppage time, grabbing a header from Mohamed Kanno to keep Saudi Arabia scoreless. Another save came in the 66th minute when he leapt to deflect a shot from Mohammed Abu Al-Shamat.

A third came in the 92nd minute when he stopped a shot by Abdullah Al-Hamdan. A group of shirtless men in the crowd each painted one letter of his name on their chests as they cheered him on.

Ana Candida Evora, mother of Cabo Verde goalkeeper Vozinha, cheers from the stands. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

But Vozinha had a much bigger fan among the crowd of 68,278 as his mother Ana Candida Evora watched from a luxury suite, waving a tiny Cabo Verde flag. It was her second match of the tournament after missing Vozinha's epic seven-save performance against Spain because of visa issues.

Cabo Verde had a chance to score in the 50th minute, but Kevin Pina's shot from distance was just above the crossbar. Another chance came in the 74th minute when Laros Duarte's shot from the middle of the box was stopped by goalkeeper Mohammed Al-Owais.

A last chance to score came in the final seconds when Nuno da Costa sent a shot from the middle of the box wide left.

But it didn't matter because a couple of minutes after the final whistle, Spain completed its victory over Uruguay and set off a joyous celebration among Cabo Verde's players and fans, many of whom cried as they rejoiced.
